title: Lockfile Reproducibility

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
Cargo.toml describes allowed versions while Cargo.lock records the exact chosen graph. Applications normally commit the lockfile so a later build does not silently select newer compatible releases.

`Cargo.toml` says which versions are acceptable; `Cargo.lock` records which exact package versions the resolver selected. If a manifest permits several compatible releases, the lockfile keeps subsequent ordinary builds on the same chosen graph until an update changes it. This helps a team reproduce a bug and compare results without silently pulling a newer dependency on every checkout.

An application normally commits its lockfile. A library crate may also commit one for its own development and tests, but downstream consumers resolve dependencies using their own lockfiles. The lockfile is therefore not a universal promise that every consumer uses the library author's exact dependency graph. If you are publishing a binary or deploying a service, review lockfile changes along with source changes, because a dependency update can alter behavior even when your own code is unchanged.

Try `cargo update -p package_name` in a disposable branch and inspect the lockfile diff. Run tests and, where relevant, a release build. To check whether a clean machine can reproduce the selected graph without modifying the lockfile, use `cargo build --locked`. Be aware that a lockfile pins versions, not the entire operating environment or external native libraries. Reproducibility improves when toolchain, build flags, and platform assumptions are recorded too.
